items.scene: At dinner, Tom casually mentions that Maya is being treated for depression in front of her new coworkers.
items.question: Was this socially inappropriate?
options: Yes, it exposed private information and could embarrass her.
No, because the information was true.
Yes, but only because it was said in a loud voice.
items.why_this_case_matters: Direct privacy violation in the wrong audience creates face threat.

items.scene: After making a rude joke about a coworker, Dana later apologizes and asks how to make it right.
items.question: What is the main issue now?
options: Whether the coworker should feel embarrassed.
items.why_this_case_matters: This is a repair-after-harm case, not a pure faux pas judgment.

items.scene: A witness says, "He left at 9 p.m.," and the investigator asks whether the witness is lying.
items.question: Is this mainly a faux pas question?
options: Yes, because it might embarrass the witness.
No, because it is mainly about whether the statement is false.
No, because it is mainly about rank and deference.
Yes, because it was said in front of others.
items.why_this_case_matters: Hard boundary: truth and deception are the main issue, not social offense.

items.scene: At a family gathering, Priya accidentally mentions that her brother recently got laid off, even though he had not told the rest of the family yet.
items.question: Was this socially inappropriate even though it was unintentional?
options: Yes, because the accidental disclosure still exposed private information.
No, because there was no intent to harm.
No, because family members can say anything to each other.
Yes, but only if the brother had already apologized.
items.why_this_case_matters: Tests the shortcut that lack of intent removes offense; social harm still matters.
